title: What a page may do to its window
summary: `client/manifest.json` declares the native window. It also grants (allows) the window controls that a service may use, under `tac.application.window.controls`. By default, no control is granted. A service gets the controls by injection, like the other browser APIs: `@Needs windowControls` in JavaScript and TypeScript, a `WindowControls` field in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Kotlin, Java, Dart, Ruby and Swift, and a `[[Needs]] WindowControls& windowControls;` field in C++. The calls are `granted(control)`, `minimize()`, `maximize()`, `fullscreen()`, `close()`, `resize(width, height)` and `setTitle(text)`, written in each language's case (`set_title` in Rust and Ruby, `SetTitle` in Go, C# and F#). A C++ call that is refused throws a `std::runtime_error`. A call to a control that is not granted fails at once, and the message names the grant to add. In a browser tab, `granted` answers `false` and every call fails, because the page has no native window. The host (the native app that shows the page) checks each grant again before it acts. The macOS host runs the controls on the app's own window, and a macOS test checks this on a real app window. The Linux (GTK) host has the controls too, and a Linux test runs the generated app under Xvfb with a window manager: a Rust page service sets the title, resizes and minimizes the app's window through the real WebKit bridge, and a close without its grant is refused. A JavaScript page caller goes through the same bridge to the same GTK controls. When the host refuses a call after it started (for example `denied`), the service hears a `BrowserCallFailed` event with `api` `windowControls`, the call's name and the host's answer as the message, as it does for a late clipboard failure. The page runtime no longer drops that answer. An iOS app has no window controls, because the system owns the window. There only `title` applies, and it sets the scene title that the iPad window switcher shows. `granted` answers `false` for every other control on iOS, and the build prints a note. On Windows, a test that needs the MSVC compiler builds the host's control code into a small program and drives a real Win32 window: it sets a granted title (with UTF-16 surrogate pairs), resizes the window, enters and leaves fullscreen and minimizes it, and checks that a close without its grant and a call from another thread are refused. That test does not open the full app or WebView2. On an Android 15 emulator, a test runs the Kotlin file shown here in the real app: the granted minimize, resize and title calls act, and maximize, fullscreen and close, which this manifest does not grant, are refused both from the page and from a Kotlin service. It has not run on a physical Android device. The page has no `globalThis.tachyonWindow` global any more, and a service that reads `globalThis` fails to build with `TY1360`. A service that the native app links in has no page, but it gets the controls from the host with the same grants (ADR 0089). The Rust file shown here works in the page and when a macOS, Linux, Windows or Android app links it, because Rust fills the field with `Default`. Swift on Apple platforms, C# on Windows and Kotlin on Android instead declare an uninitialized `WindowControls` field with `NeedsAll`. Their native files are under native/, a documentation folder; the file you choose goes in the application's client/services/. Native service code belongs to the application. It runs as normal operating-system code, and this window-control policy does not sandbox (limit) it. Lua and Python services have no `WindowControls` yet, so this feature has no tab for them: a Lua field of this type stops the build with `TY2015`, and Python stops it with `TY1605` (`WindowControls` is not a model). Let a service in another language handle the window.
